newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: SERBIA HOPES ECON STABILITY WILL ENCOURAGE GROWTH.
newsitem.headline: SERBIA HOPES ECON STABILITY WILL ENCOURAGE GROWTH.

text.p: Serbia's Prime Minister Mirko Marjanovic on Monday extolled the country's price and currency stability, saying he hoped it would encourage business activity and translate into higher industry output and exports.

"Only price and currency stability creates an environment encouraging everyone to operate on market principles and be profit-oriented while increasing production and exports," Marjanovic said in written answers to Reuter questions.

"Prices have been entirely stabilised so that their average monthly growth is below one percent. The dinar exchange rate has also been stable with a very narrow spread between its official and market rates. Price and currency stability resulted in higher industry production and exports," he said.
Retail prices fell 0.1 percent in June, after growing at a modest 0.1 or 0.2 percent monthly rate in April and May. The cumulative rate of growth in industrial output in January-May was 7.8 percent.
The dinar is officially fixed at 3.3 to the German mark, while its market rate idles between 3.5 and 3.7 for months.
Marjanovic said Serbia was taking additional steps to strengthen economic stability while stimulating production and exports.
"It is vital to maintain full fiscal discipline and balance public spending and public revenues, which eliminates the key cause of inflation and overall economic instability," he added.

Serbia is upgrading its infrastructure, raising output in its metal-processing industries (based on gas and oil barter deals with Russia and China) and encouraging agricultural production, Marjanovic said.

Almost $1 billion raised from a strategic partnership deal with Italian and Greek telecom companies STET and OTE, who bought 49 percent stake in the Telekom Srbija, will be used for development purposes, he added.
Despite recent output growth, Yugoslavian industrial output remains 52.8 percent below its 1991 level when the former federation broke up.

Low capacity utilisation is pushing production costs up and a lack of working capital and expensive commercial bank lending is difficult to replace from other sources while Yugoslavia remains barred from world capital markets.

"Sanctions have only recently been lifted and the outer wall of sanctions is still obstructing our access to international markets and full employment and (higher) capacity utilisation," Marjanovic said.
A problem of burgeoning inter-company debt was expected to be relaxed now that the federal parliament adopted a law on inter-company debt settlement.
Yugoslav firms have accumulated almost 7 billion in inter-company debt since 1994, when Yugoslavia started from scratch after a year of hyperinflation of 60 percent a day.
Meanwhile, the government has offered temporary tax relief to most threatened industry sectors and the postponement payments of tax contributions for several months.
The government will also launch a scheme to tackle the problem of surplus labour.

"Along with the forthcoming ownership transformation, the government will prepare a comprehensive social programme aimed at relieving companies of surplus labour in an economically and socially acceptable manner. This will also bring substantial relief to the companies' working capital." Marjanovic said.

"We have also progressed in preparing pension and health system reforms introducing market criteria...This will lead to a more stable inflow of money to social security funds without additionally burdening the economy," he said.
Marjanovic insisted the government has done everything to avoid central bank financing to cover public spending, forecast at 47.5 percent of the country's gross domestic product.
Economists forecast Yugoslavia's 1996 GDP at around 17 billion. Serbia accounts for 95 percent of it.
"Serbia is making every effort to secure funds for public spending from real sources only, without resorting to the central bank," he said. REUTER
